This page is the human-readable face of a citable record: the archived dataset carries the driver,
the geometry, the cluster scripts, every raw result and the analysis that turns them into these
tables. It states what **peclet.flow 1.0.0** does on the hardware it was measured on. It is
not a comparison against other codes, and it makes no claim about any other version.

::: {.callout-note title="Amended 2026-09-15"}
The measurements are unchanged. Three readings of them were corrected after a companion campaign
(`benchmarks/momentum-solver`, archived alongside this record) re-ran the CPU ladder with the
momentum solver pinned: the 1536-core gate difference is a **capped** momentum solve
against a converged one; the 16-GPU anomaly's decomposition-shape hypothesis is
**withdrawn**, contradicted by this record's own rungs; and the weak ladder's projection growth is
**not** the global reduction, which the timers put at 0.6 % of the phase. Each
correction is marked in place below. Nothing here revises a timing, an efficiency or the
permeability.
:::

## What is measured

**Creeping flow through a periodic random sphere packing, with the cut-cell immersed boundary
method**, driven by a body force in a triply periodic box. One MPI rank per GPU or per core.

The physical unit of the study is a **unit cell**: 1043 spheres of radius $R = 1$ at solid fraction
$\phi = 0.45$ in a cubic box of $21.333\,R$, resolved at $384^3$ cells — so $R = 18$ cells,
comfortably inside the resolution at which this discretization's permeability has converged. That
cell is 56.6 M cells, and it is what one H100 holds.

Four ladders, one case:

| Ladder | Machine | What changes | Rungs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Weak** | Snellius `gpu_h100` | one unit cell **per GPU**, the domain grows with the GPU count | 1 → 32 GPUs, 56.6 M → 1.81 Gcells |
| **Strong (CPU)** | Snellius `genoa` | one fixed unit cell, more cores | 24 → 1536 cores |
| **Strong (GPU)** | Snellius `gpu_h100` | one fixed unit cell, more GPUs | 1 → 32 GPUs |
| **Control** | both | Taylor–Green vortices, no geometry, same grids | subset |

The weak ladder **tiles one unit cell**. Rung $N$ is an exact periodic replication of the same
problem, $N$ times over — the porous-media analogue of tiling vortices. That choice is what makes
the physics observable exact rather than statistical: the tiled problem *is* the same problem, so
its answer must be the same number, and any disagreement is a defect rather than bed-to-bed
scatter.

## Correctness first

Every run starts from rest and takes the same 13 steps, so the mean velocity
$\langle u \rangle$ at the end is one number that every rung must return — at any rank count, on
either machine. It costs one global reduction, and it is checked for every run in the record.

::: {.callout-important title="One state, 30 runs, two machines"}
$\langle u \rangle = 1.638889605549e-04$

across **30 runs** spanning 1 to 768 ranks, both the CUDA and the OpenMP
backend, single-rank and distributed, and domains from 56.6 M to
1.81 billion cells. Worst relative deviation **8e−11**; peak divergence
3e-14. The geometry-free control is tighter still: **1e−16** — machine
epsilon — over 6 runs to 768 ranks.
:::

That is the claim the timings rest on. A fast rung that has quietly stopped solving the same
problem is worth nothing, so the equivalence is established first and the performance is read only
from runs that pass it.

**Where the record does *not* return one number, and why.** At 1536 cores this problem
is down to 37 k cells per rank, and peclet 1.0.0 switches its momentum
solver by itself below ~65 k — so those rungs run the velocity multigrid where the rest of the
ladder does not. A different solver is a different iterate, and the two land
**3.7e−07** apart in $\langle u \rangle$. That is a configuration difference rather than a
parallel-consistency one, and the evidence is that it is perfectly repeatable: 3
separate 1536-core allocations return values identical to the last digit
(spread 0). The gate table groups by solver configuration for this reason.

::: {.callout-important title="Amended 2026-09-15: the two values are a capped solve and a converged one"}
A companion campaign (`benchmarks/momentum-solver`) re-ran this CPU ladder with the momentum
solver **pinned** at every rung instead of left to the automatic rule, and recorded the sweep count
the solver already reports and this record did not keep. On **every** rung of the CPU ladder the
red-black momentum solve runs **200 sweeps per component — its iteration cap
(`velIters_`)** — while the velocity multigrid converges in 9.7. So the
3.7e−07 above is not two converged solutions of the same equation reached by different
routes: it is a **capped** solve against a **converged** one, and the multigrid value is the
converged one.

Nothing in the timings below changes — they remain what peclet 1.0.0 does with its shipped
defaults, which is the question this record set out to answer. What changes is the reading: the
cross-rung equivalence gate demonstrates **reproducibility**, which it genuinely has to
8e−11, and not convergence of the momentum solve.

**The GPU ladders are at the cap as well** (200 sweeps per component on one H100
and on four). That is established rather than inferred: the pinned red-black run reproduces this
record's own 1-GPU rung to 1.0006×, so it *is* that rung. Pinning the velocity
multigrid instead takes the same 1-GPU step from 4025 to **1840 ms**
(2.19×, with the momentum phase alone 3.64× faster), and the 4-GPU
step from 1203 to 664 ms (1.81×). Every figure in this
record is therefore a measurement of 1.0.0's default momentum solver running at its iteration cap
— which is what a user gets, and roughly a factor of two off what the same code does with
`set_velocity_multigrid(True)`.
:::

## Weak scaling — the distributed solve

![Per-GPU throughput and pressure iterations, 1 → 32 H100 GPUs at $384^3$ cells each.](weak_scaling.png)

Per-GPU throughput goes from **14.1** to **11.2 Mcell/s** between 1 and
32 GPUs: **79 % weak efficiency** at 1.81 billion cells, an
aggregate 358 Mcell/s. The pressure solve takes **29.7 iterations per
step at 1 GPU and 29.8 at 32** — flat, which is the property that matters: a
weak ladder whose iteration count climbs is not weak-scaling, however level its throughput curve
looks. The multigrid hierarchy reaches 8 levels and the coarse levels telescope onto
fewer ranks as they shrink, so the coarsest grid stays solvable however many ranks the fine grid
is spread over.

**On the absolute throughput (amended 2026-09-15).** The Mcell/s figures here are 1.0.0's default
momentum solver, which is at its iteration cap (above); the same problem on one H100 runs
2.19× faster with the velocity multigrid pinned. The **efficiency** is a ratio of
like to like and is not affected — but a reader sizing hardware from the throughput numbers should
know there is about a factor of two of headroom in them, and that it is one API call away. Nor is
the efficiency a figure to carry across versions once that call becomes the default — see
[Reading the numbers fairly](#reading-the-numbers-fairly).

## Strong scaling — one fixed problem

![The same 56.6 M-cell problem, on more cores and on more GPUs.](strong_scaling.png)

On CPU, 24 → 1536 cores takes the step from 71.1 s to **0.91 s**,
a **78.0×** speedup — nominally 122 % of ideal, which is above 100 % and
should not be read as the solver beating linear scaling. Two things inflate it, and both are worth
naming rather than banking. The 24-core baseline has the whole node's memory bandwidth to
itself, so it is a flattered reference; and at 1536 cores the automatic rule switches
the momentum solver (above), so the top rung runs a *different and better* algorithm — 768 →
1536 alone returns 3.3× for a doubling. The honest reading is that this problem strong-scales
well across the whole CPU ladder, not that it exceeds ideal.

::: {.callout-important title="Amended 2026-09-15: how much of it was the solver switch"}
The companion pinned-solver ladder answers this quantitatively. Run with one algorithm from
24 to 1536 cores, the ladder reads **50.8×
(79 % of ideal) for red-black Gauss-Seidel** and **26.4×
(41 %) for the velocity multigrid** — each the honest scaling of a single algorithm,
and neither above 100 %. The 122 % figure above is what you get by measuring a capped
solver at the bottom of a ladder and a converged one at the top.

The same ladder says the multigrid is the better momentum solver **at every rank count**, not only
below the threshold where 1.0.0 switches to it: it wins by 1.66× to
2.23× across the 6 rungs up to 768 cores, and
its margin is *largest* at the biggest blocks (2.23× at 384 cores,
147 k cells per rank) — the opposite of the threshold's premise, and still
2.23× ahead at 2.36 M cells per rank. That is a defect in a shipped
default rather than a property of this benchmark, and it is recorded here because a reader sizing a
job from these numbers should know that `set_velocity_multigrid(True)` is worth roughly a factor of
two on CPU across this whole range, and 2.19× on one H100.

The 1536-core rung is deliberately **left out of that range**. It is the rung this study
found least reproducible: 3 separate allocations of the identical multigrid
configuration spread **2.01×**, against 1.06× for red-black over
2. At 37 k cells per rank the step is short enough that node
placement, not the solver, is what a single allocation measures — which is the same reason the two
strong-scaling efficiencies above are quoted from medians over repeats and should be read as
approximate.
:::

On GPU the same problem goes from 4.0 s on one H100 to **0.55 s on 32**
(7.3×, 23 % of ideal). The efficiency falls off where it should: at
32 GPUs each device holds only 1.8 M cells, far below what saturates an
H100, and the step becomes a latency problem rather than a throughput one. **That is the honest
limit of strong scaling on this hardware, and it is why the weak ladder is the headline** — a GPU
earns its keep on a large subdomain, and the fixed problem here fits on one of them to begin with.

One rung does not behave, and it is reproducible. At **16 GPUs the step is slower than at
8** (926 ms against 857 ms) — 2 separate
allocations agree to 1.00×, so this is not node placement. The phase timers put all of it
in the **projection**: 303 → 514 ms while the momentum solve keeps scaling
(553 → 411 ms), with an identical multigrid hierarchy at both rungs. The
decomposition shape is the obvious suspect — 8 GPUs give every rank a cubic block
(192x192x192), 16 give it a 1:2:2 one (96x192x192).

**That suspicion does not survive this record's own data, and is withdrawn (2026-09-15).** The
32-GPU rung has a *more* elongated block (96x96x192) and a *worse* surface-to-volume
ratio (0.0521 against 0.0417 at 16 and 0.0312 at 8 —
`hierarchy_predict.txt`), and it is the **fastest** rung on the ladder at 552 ms. A
monotone quantity cannot produce a non-monotone dip. What the measurements do establish is a list
of what the anomaly is *not*: not node placement (2 allocations, different node
sets, agreeing to 1.00×); not the momentum phase, which is on trend
(553 → 411 → 284 ms); not the iteration count, flat at
29.7; and not the global reduction, which the timers put at 4.1 ms,
0.8 % of the projection. Nor is it the multigrid hierarchy: all three rungs build
8 levels, and the slow rung at 16 GPUs and the fastest one at 32
have *identical* structure down to the level at which the coarse grids telescope onto fewer ranks
(L5 for both; 8 GPUs, the other fast rung, telescopes one level later — see
`hierarchy_predict.txt`). The two rungs that bracket the anomaly therefore differ from it in
opposite directions on every structural quantity available. The
anomaly is real, reproducible, confined to the projection, and undiagnosed.

Taken together the two machines price the same work: on this case one H100 is worth roughly
**348 Genoa cores**. That is the conservative reading — the CPU is credited with the
best per-core throughput anywhere on its ladder, which is its 1536-core rung, the
one that also benefits from the momentum-solver switch. Against its weakest rung the ratio is
several times larger.

## Where the step goes

![Per-phase median times across the weak ladder.](phase_breakdown.png)

The step is two solves and a negligible explicit stage (the predictor is 5.1 ms,
about a tenth of a percent). Across the weak ladder the **momentum solve grows
12 %** (3013 → 3372 ms from 1 to 32
GPUs) while the **pressure projection grows 68 %**
(1006 → 1687 ms). The iteration count is flat, so the gap is
not a convergence effect.

**Amended 2026-09-15.** This record previously read that gap as "where the global coupling lives".
Its own timers do not support that: the pressure all-reduce is 10.5 ms at the top rung
against a 1687 ms projection — **0.6 %** — and its growth from
0.32 ms accounts for a comparably small share of the increase. The global reduction is
not where the weak ladder loses. Two things that are: the V-cycle's coarse levels are
latency-bound, each costing a halo exchange on a grid too small to amortise it; and the hierarchy
**deepens along the ladder**, from 8 levels at 1 GPU to 10 at
32, because weak scaling grows the global grid — so part of that growth is extra levels
per V-cycle and is not a parallel inefficiency at all.

A second correction of emphasis. The projection carries the weak ladder's *loss*, but the momentum
solve carries the *time*: it is 75 % of the step at 1 GPU and
67 % at 32. Removing the projection's entire weak-scaling excess
would save less than halving the momentum solve would — and on CPU, pinning the momentum solver
does roughly that (above). Both statements are true and this record originally made only the
first.

## The geometry-free control

The Taylor–Green control runs the identical grids and the identical decomposition with no geometry
at all. It is **not** a measurement of what the immersed boundary costs, and should not be read as
one: the control solves an advecting flow while the bed case is creeping (advection off), so the
two differ in the physics as well as in the geometry.

What it does isolate is the solver floor and the shape of the scaling. Two things follow. The
cut-cell pressure operator needs **3.7×** the iterations of the all-fluid one
(29.7 against 8.0), which is what a matrix whose coefficients span the
aperture contrast of a dense bed costs. And the whole step nevertheless lands within
**1.0×** of the control's, because the control spends on advection roughly what the bed
spends on its stiffer pressure solve. The control also weak-scales slightly better
(88 % against 79 % at 32 GPUs), which puts a number on how much
of the loss at the top of the ladder is the geometry's irregular work rather than the
communication both cases share.

## Permeability

Marched to steady state, the unit cell has $k/R^2 = 0.017122$ (40 steps to a
relative tolerance of $10^{-5}$). Measured at 5 points of the ladder, the estimates agree
to 5e−13 — the same physical answer from the single-GPU cell and from the tiled
1.81-billion-cell domain.

## Reading the numbers fairly

- The CPU rungs take **exclusive** nodes, so the sub-node rungs (24, 48, 96) have up to
  8× the memory bandwidth per rank of the full-node rungs. That flatters the baseline and therefore
  **understates** the efficiencies computed against it; the apples-to-apples segment is 192 →
  1536.
- The weak ladder's large rungs are **periodic replications** of one unit cell, not independent
  beds. That is what makes the physics gate exact; it is not a statement about bed-to-bed
  variability.
- Timings are the **median** of 10 timed steps after 3 warm-up steps, taken
  as the slowest rank's wall time for each step. The per-run spread is in the tables; repeats of
  the top rungs on separate allocations are reported separately, because node placement moves a
  large-rank number by more than the solver does.
- The configuration is the **shipped 1.0.0 default** — MG-PCG at a relative tolerance of
  $10^{-8}$, coarse-level telescoping, the agglomerated coarse solve, the velocity-multigrid auto
  rule, double operator storage, and the shipped auto-detection of GPU-aware MPI — with **one
  stated exception**: the pressure multigrid is asked for as much depth as the grid admits rather
  than the default of four levels. Depth is a property of the grid, not a tuning constant. The
  out-of-the-box depth is measured at one rung and is in the tables.
- **This is a record of 1.0.0, and the default it measures has since changed.** 1.0.0
  chose the momentum solver by cells per rank; from the next release it is chosen by the
  implicit-diffusion operator's condition number, $\kappa = 1 + 12D$ isotropic, with the velocity
  multigrid taken at $\kappa \ge 13$. **Every run in this record is at $D = 6$, so $\kappa = 73$**
  — a later version runs this whole study with the velocity multigrid, the solver pinned by hand
  above, and is therefore *faster* on this case than every absolute figure here by about the
  headroom quoted. The **efficiencies** move the other way and are the ones to carry forward
  carefully: the momentum phase is 75 % of the step at 1 GPU and grows
  12 % across the weak ladder against the projection's
  68 %, so making momentum 3.64× cheaper shifts the step
  toward the phase that scales worst. This record's own pinned ladder measures that trade directly:
  on 24 → 1536 cores, red-black reads 79 % of ideal and the velocity multigrid
  41 %. The 79 % weak efficiency here is 1.0.0's, at
  1.0.0's default; what a later default achieves on this case is **not measured in this
  record**.
- `PECLET_CORE_GPU_AWARE_MPI` is deliberately left unset, so the shipped auto-detection decides the
  halo transport and the runs record what it chose: on this machine, **DEVICE MPI buffers (auto)**.
- Runs whose pressure solve touched its iteration cap would be reported as capped rather than
  plotted as timings. None did: the worst rung used a small fraction of the cap.

## Reproduce it

The published wheels cannot run this — MPI is a build-time option in `flow` and the PyPI wheels are
single-rank — so the study builds the released tag from source, with one tree per backend.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/computational-chemical-engineering/peclet-examples
cd peclet-examples/benchmarks/release-1.0.0-scaling

sbatch --nodes=1 --gpus-per-node=1 --ntasks-per-node=1 snellius/install_bench.sh v1.0.0 h100
sbatch -p genoa --gpus-per-node=0 -c 32 -t 02:00:00    snellius/install_bench.sh v1.0.0 cpu

./snellius/submit_ladders.sh pilot     # the go/no-go rungs
./snellius/submit_ladders.sh weak      # and strong-gpu, strong-cpu, tgv, march, spread, levels
python analyze.py results              # tables, gates, figures
```

The runbook is [`README.md`](https://github.com/computational-chemical-engineering/peclet-examples/blob/main/benchmarks/release-1.0.0-scaling/README.md); the design decisions, including the ones that
were rejected, are in [`DECISIONS.md`](https://github.com/computational-chemical-engineering/peclet-examples/blob/main/benchmarks/release-1.0.0-scaling/DECISIONS.md). The whole directory — driver, geometry,
cluster scripts, raw results and logs — is
[on GitHub](https://github.com/computational-chemical-engineering/peclet-examples/tree/main/benchmarks/release-1.0.0-scaling).
